steps.do: Register the policy tool. The wizard has five steps: Identity, Implementation, Schema, Playground, Safety & Review. A registered tool must point at importable Python, so you give a Module Path and a Callable Name from the shipped demo module. On the Schema step use each schema's Raw JSON toggle and paste input_schema and output_schema from the asset.
fill: on, so the sandbox runs the real callable
steps.see: The tool opens on its detail page. Back in the Tools list its row has no Built-in or Unavailable label: those mark CALIBER's own tools. Registering opens the tool's detail page: its Open the workspace link leads to Sandbox, Fixtures, Hardening and Test Runs (the address becomes /tools?tool=TL-…, so a reload keeps you there).

steps.do: Register the write tool the same way. On the Safety & Review step click Write: Requires Approval switches on and is locked, because the registry refuses a write tool without it. (Through the API that refusal is an HTTP 400.)
steps.see: initiate_refund is registered with Requires Approval on and cannot be turned off.

steps.do: Open the tool from the Tools list, then the Sandbox tab. Run the policy with the first fixture's inputs. Then open initiate_refund and run it: a write tool is never called in the sandbox.
steps.see: Success with decision: approve, reason_code: ELIGIBLE_AUTO_APPROVE. For the write tool: Success (mocked) and the output {"_preview_mock": true}.

steps.do: Load the 49 cases from the dataset file: Load cases from file, choose refund-fixtures.jsonl. Each line becomes a case named R01 small delivered order, with the line's inputs as the input JSON and an equals assertion on its expectations (key order and spacing do not matter). Loading only fills the editor; nothing is stored until you save. You can also add or edit single cases by hand with Add case.
steps.see: Loaded 49 cases from refund-fixtures.jsonl. Save cases to keep them., then Saved after you save, and 49 case rows in the editor (still 49 after a reload).

steps.do: Run the saved suite. It scores inline, one subprocess per case, so 49 cases take about half a minute. A run is recorded under Test Runs automatically.
steps.see: Pass rate 100% — 49/49 passed and a green pass on every case.

steps.do: Open Test Runs and pin the latest run. Then go back to Hardening, change the expected value of case R09 (approve) to manual_review / AMOUNT_OVER_THRESHOLD / true, and run the suite again. Put the value back afterwards and run once more.
steps.see: The pinned run carries a Baseline marker. The second run reads Pass rate 98% — 48/49 passed; under Test Runs the comparison shows 1 regression on R09 and Net score -2%.

steps.do: Import the workflow asset. If you registered the tools under other names, replace decide_refund and initiate_refund in the file first. Validate dependencies checks that both tools resolve.
steps.see: Preflight passed, both tools resolved; then the editor opens on the new draft.

steps.do: Run a case, then try to approve it yourself. In a second browser session sign in as approver1, pick the same workspace, open the workflow, Run Monitor, select the run in Recent runs and approve. Back in the first session, Resume. The gate is the refund tool's own approval flag.
fill: the R01 inputs, as in the Sandbox step
steps.see: The run stops at Awaiting approval on node refund. Your own Approve is refused (a second person must decide). After approver1 approves, Resume enables; after it the run is completed and the output shows refund_status: initiated, amount_usd: 49.0.

steps.where: Workflows › refund-decision › Run Monitor, then Audit Log
steps.do: Start two more runs: one with the R01 inputs that approver1 rejects, one with the R23 inputs (a cancelled order). Then open Audit Log.
steps.see: The rejected run is failed and its output holds no refund. The R23 run completed with decision: deny and never asked for approval. Audit Log lists approve_workflow_run_runtime_approval and reject_workflow_run_runtime_approval by approver1, and resume_workflow_run by the initiator.
